name: Missing Criteria - Critical Requirements
definition:
Missing Criteria - Critical Requirements Definition:
Count each missing rubric that ought to check for an explicit requirement in the prompt or a critical implicit expectation of the prompt as one issue (critical = you cannot imagine a good response without it)

Each hallucination annotation should have a dedicated criterion covering the issue. If not, count it as one issue.


CBs are expected to provide up to 5 spot checks if there are sufficiently similar outcomes as well as add a criterion to check the volume of the outcomes.
If too many criteria spot-check one group, report it once as Too Many Spot Checks.

Each missing volume check would count as a missing criteria

Each group’s missing spot checks would count as a singular missing criteria


Example 1:
Output: provides 200 emails

Rubric: Has 3 criteria that check random emails among the list + a criterion that checks that “the model sends at least 200 replies”


NOTE: Remember that the rubric is one-half of the verification suite—you should also consider unit test coverage when determining whether a requirement is fulfilled. The fundamental concept is that unit tests should cover binary, “mechanical” assertions, while the rubric is intended to capture more nuanced details which cannot easily be verified by unit tests. Do not penalize a “missing criterion” if it is included within the unit tests, unless there is an important qualifier of the request that cannot be assessed mechanically via unit testing.
Example:
Acceptable:

Prompt: “Send a message to my mom.”

Rubric: Has no criteria regarding this message.

Unit test: Checks if a message was sent to the user’s mom.

The rubric should not be penalized for “missing criteria” since this is captured by the unit test.

Penalizable:

Prompt: “Send a message to my mom telling her that I really loved her cookie recipe.”

Rubric: Has no criteria regarding this message.

Unit test: Checks if a message was sent to the user’s mom.

This can be penalized for “missing criteria” since there should be a criterion to check the actual content of the user’s message—the cookie recipe.
boundary: A negative criterion covers the requirement it guards. Penalising the wrong answer is a way of requiring the right one, so do not file a requirement as uncovered on the ground that the only criterion reaching it is negative and fires solely on the defect: that is what a negative criterion is, and the half of this project that measures hallucination rests on exactly those. Weigh it as coverage, and where it is outweighed by the positives around it say so as a weighting observation rather than as a missing criterion. Do not file a finding you have argued yourself out of. Where you can state the reason this rubric needs no such criterion -- the outcomes are already enumerated one by one, the panel that discriminates the answer is the one checked, the prompt gives the material as background rather than asking the response to describe it -- that reason is the verdict, and the requirement is covered. Erring toward reporting governs how much evidence a finding needs, and never turns a criterion you have cleared into a finding. A hallucination annotation is one the trajectory carries, not a trap the ground truth anticipated. The definition asks for a dedicated criterion per hallucination annotation, and an annotation is a wrong claim the model actually made on this run -- the dimension it belongs to is scored on the hallucinations present in the trajectory. An entry under 'what should mislead a careless model' that the run never committed is an anticipated trap, and hallucination criteria are allowed to go untriggered, so a rubric carrying no criterion for one is not missing a criterion. Where the trajectory carries a different wrong claim about the same material, the annotation to look for a criterion against is the one that fired. This narrows the annotation door and nothing else: a requirement the prompt states, or a critical implicit expectation of it, is covered by the first sentence of the definition whether or not the ground truth also lists it as a mislead. Similar outcomes are a group, and the definition asks for a sample of one rather than a check on each of its members. Where the rubric and the unit tests between them sample a group -- spot checks on some members with a criterion on the volume or the shape of the whole -- the group is covered, and a further member is what the definition tells authors not to add rather than a missing criterion: past five spot checks for a group it is Too Many Spot Checks. Count a group's missing spot checks as one issue, never one per member and never one per column of a fixed-shape output file. The unit tests are the other half of the verification suite, so a requirement they assert mechanically is covered and is not a missing criterion. This clears a further member of a group the suite already samples and nothing else: a requirement the prompt states as its own limb, that no criterion and no test reaches in either direction, is not a member of some other group's sample, and a cap reached elsewhere is no reason to clear it.

name: Criteria Not Self Contained
definition:
Not Self Contained Definition: 
Criterion cannot be evaluated against the model response without access to the prompt, reference text, other criteria, and/or external facts/information


Every rubric must be self-contained. Imagine that you only have access to the model response (including its trajectory) and are trying to evaluate if it fulfilled the rubric item. Will you be able to evaluate accurately without referencing anything else? Some criteria are self-explanatory but often, this translates to the criteria mentioning the answer to the prompt directly.

Examples of criteria that are not self-contained:
Example 1: “Response identifies the first president of the USA"

Fixed: "Response identifies the first president of the USA as George Washington"

Example 2: “The response addresses the bug mentioned in the prompt"

Fixed: "The response addresses the bug where the submit button doesn't work"
-------------------------------------------------

**Note / Limited Exception:**
A criterion may be treated as not counted for self-containment when fully enumerating all relevant workspace-specific values, quantities, filenames, or similar facts would be impractical, **provided that the criterion is supplementary and the underlying failure outcome is independently captured by other self-contained criteria**.

For example, this may apply when the downstream correct values the model is expected to state are already covered by more than one positive completion criteria. When it applies, it is not counted as a major issue, and is noted instead.
boundary: Apply the test the definition sets, as it states it: holding only this criterion and the model response, could a grader evaluate it accurately without referencing anything else -- not the prompt, not the reference text, not another criterion, not a fact from outside. That is two questions, and the criterion has to answer both in its own words: what is being measured, and what counts as right. Take the definition's own parenthetical seriously -- the response includes its trajectory, and so includes what the model did and the files it left behind. A criterion about an action rather than an assertion is therefore gradable: whether a file was opened, whether a figure was viewed before being cited, whether a script was run, and what the model's own output files contain are all in front of the grader. Judging those against the answer text alone finds them targetless and files a Major against a criterion that grades perfectly well. A value on its own does not say what is measured. "Response reports the difference is 0.153 Å" carries a number and no subject: the difference between which two quantities is settled in another criterion, so a grader holding only this one cannot tell a response's 0.153 of the right difference from a coincidence. The same holds for a value hung on a referring phrase -- "the found distance", "Lewiński's value", "that velocity", "the above" -- whose referent is fixed by the prompt or a neighbouring criterion rather than by this one; a criterion that reads only as a continuation of the one before it is this defect. Fixed, it names its subject: "Response states that the shortest aryl H···Ga contact it found (Ga1···H70, 2.960 Å, in 4MeRyBDIGaNNFl) is 0.153 Å longer than the Ga1···H14 contact of 2.807 Å in Lewiński's [(MeAl)2(naphtha)(CN)2(GaMe3)2]". A criterion that names the atoms, the compound, the file or the entity it is about together with what it wants -- "identifies Lewiński's distance as between Ga1 and H14 on C14 in [(MeAl)2(naphtha)(CN)2(GaMe3)2]" -- is self-contained. Alternatives defined by material the criterion does not identify are the same defect. "Or equivalent from the .cif file" leaves the grader to find out which file and what it holds, which is referencing something else; the fix names the file, or states the accepted alternatives. A negative criterion naming a class of wrong claims is held to this test for its subject and for what puts a claim in the class, not for an inventory of the class's members. "Response identifies acetate or a downstream product of acetate kinase as produced by the current cascade" says what is measured and what makes a claim wrong, in its own words and the field's ordinary terms, so a grader holding it can tell whether a response's claim falls in the class. Listing every member would make the criterion harder to read and to grade, and a negative is there to catch the failure however a run phrases it. A negative whose class is fixed only by material it does not identify -- "states any figure the workspace does not support" -- still leaves the grader to consult that material, and is the defect. That the prompt or the workspace would settle the question for a grader who consulted them does not answer this test, since the definition asks whether the criterion can be evaluated without them. What is not the defect is the work of checking a response against a criterion that already says what it wants: a criterion stating its subject and its value is self-contained however long it takes to confirm the response matches. So a finding says what a grader holding only this criterion and the response could not tell -- the subject, the target, or which alternatives count -- and names what they would have to consult to tell it. The definition's Limited Exception is part of it and is narrow. It applies only where fully enumerating the workspace-specific values would be impractical -- a list too long to write out, not one value or a pair the criterion could have named -- and only where the criterion is supplementary and the failure it guards is independently captured by other criteria that are themselves self-contained. Name those criteria; one that fails this test itself captures nothing. A criterion carrying a value the answer turns on -- a figure, an identification or a comparison the prompt asks for -- is not supplementary, and the exception never reaches it. Where the exception applies, record the criterion in `notes` as not counted rather than filing it; where you cannot name the covering criteria, the exception does not apply and the criterion is judged like any other.

name: Criteria Not Atomic - Major
definition:
Ask yourself, “Can two model responses of differing quality be scored equally under this criterion due to bundling of deliverables?” The idea is to test whether the response could satisfy one part of the criterion and fail another. If it could, the criterion is bundling behaviors and should be flagged.

To determine whether the error is Major or Moderate, consider how related the items being bundled are. If the items are all regarding the same deliverable or subject, then the error is Moderate; otherwise, it is major.

Example criterion with a Major error: “The model creates the .csv file named "analysis_results.csv" and states that the 1,169 bp band corresponds to the Sh ble cassette.”
  Major error: Criterion refers to both the file and the bp band statement.

Example criterion with a Moderate error: “The model creates the .csv file named "analysis_results.csv" containing the results of the CBA for a second research lab.”
  Moderate error: Criterion refers to both the creation of a file and its contents.

If both a Major and Moderate atomicity error are present within one criterion, only count the Major error.
Example criterion with both a Major AND Moderate error: “The model creates the .csv file named "analysis_results.csv" containing the results of the CBA for a second research lab and states that the 1,169 bp band corresponds to the Sh ble cassette.”

This does not apply when a single criterion introduces an item and specifies the property that identifies it. ("States that the 1,169 bp colony-PCR band corresponds to the Sh ble cassette conferring zeocin resistance" is acceptable.)
boundary: The test is the definition's own question, and a finding has to answer it concretely: name the two parts, and the response that splits them by delivering one and not the other, so that it earns the same verdict as a response delivering neither. Where you can, the criterion bundles deliverables whatever the parts have in common. The allowance this category once made for parts serving one general idea is withdrawn: the definition's Moderate example -- a file created and its contents -- is two parts of one deliverable. The severity follows from how related the parts are: about the same deliverable or subject is Moderate, about different ones is Major, and a criterion carrying both is filed once, as Major. What is not a second part: a criterion that introduces an item and states what the item is or what it does -- its function, its role, the reaction it catalyses -- is one thing, as the definition's own acceptable example is: the band 'corresponds to the Sh ble cassette conferring zeocin resistance'. That holds even where the item's name alone would already tell a grader which item is meant: the Sh ble cassette is unambiguous without its resistance, and the two still read as one claim. What stays a second part is a further finding about the item that the response has to reach from this task's material -- a value it takes here, a verdict on it, a behaviour peculiar to this task such as an enzyme running in the reverse of its usual direction -- since a response can name the item and what it does and never reach that finding. The name a file must carry and the unit a value is stated in are not second parts either: they say how the one deliverable is recognised. A negative criterion's firing condition is not a list of deliverables either: where its parts together describe one wrong claim, such as a label and the figure that shows the label wrong, there is no part a response can satisfy on its own. Where the parts are two wrong claims a response can make separately, it is judged like any other criterion.

name: Subjective Criteria
definition:
Subjective Definition:
Criteria that are subjective, vague or immeasurable (e.g., “the response should have good formatting” or “code must be optimal”)

A criterion should be evaluated based on whether its primary requirement is measurable, even if it includes additional context or reasoning that's less precise

Using vague or subjective qualifiers like “appropriate”, “properly”, “best practices”, “reasonable” etc without attaching explicit definitions makes criteria unmeasurable and should be flagged here.

Subjectivity with certain details should be acceptable when the prompt is intentionally ambiguous and open-ended
For example, for a prompt "Create an artistic website to showcase my sculptures, featuring an animated background that looks like shifting, fluid marble", the following rubric is acceptable: "The website has a refined modern look so it could be launched as a product by a reputable company."
boundary: The definition names the case outright: a vague or subjective qualifier with no explicit definition attached makes a criterion unmeasurable. A comparison or judgement the criterion asks for with no standard attached -- "close", "comparable", "similar", "consistent with", "significant", "in good agreement" -- is that qualifier: two graders holding the same response and the same values can reach opposite verdicts on whether 2.960 Å and 2.807 Å are close. Name the qualifier and the standard it lacks; the fix states the standard -- a tolerance, a threshold, a named convention -- or drops the qualifier and asks for the fact. Its bounds are the definition's own two. The criterion is judged on its primary requirement, so a qualifier in context or reasoning around a requirement that is itself measurable is not a finding. And subjectivity is acceptable where the prompt is intentionally open-ended in the way the definition's example is -- a creative brief rather than a question with a determined answer.

name: Double Negative
definition:
Double Negative Definition:
A negative criteria penalizes something absent from the response instead of rewarding an equivalent thing being present


Example: “The response does not do ABC” weighted as -1, -3, or -5.

name: Dense or Ambiguous Phrasing
definition:
Dense or Ambiguous Phrasing Definition:
Criterion is correct and measurable, but its wording admits more than one reading, or it leans on context the criterion does not state. Be careful not to confuse this error with "Criteria Not Self Contained" or "Subjective Criteria"; there is a note at the end of this description to help distinguish these three error types.

Ask yourself whether two graders holding only this criterion would grade the same response differently. If they would, the wording is the defect and it should be flagged here.

This covers ordinals and implicit sequence references. A criterion that names its subject as "the second recombination", "the other cassette" or "the remaining clone" points at a position in a sequence the criterion never states, and which one is meant depends on how the reader happened to order the material. Name the thing by the name the prompt and the workspace use.

It also covers wording dense enough that the verdict turns on which clause attaches to what, where splitting the sentence in two would settle the question without changing what is being asked for.

The defect is in the wording rather than in what the criterion checks.

Count each criterion with ambiguous wording as one moderate issue.

NOTE: A criterion that is long or uses domain terminology is acceptable as long as it has one reading. When flagging, state both readings and give a response that one reading accepts and the other rejects.

NOTE: Where the criterion cannot be evaluated against the response at all without the prompt, reference text or other criteria, use "Criteria Not Self Contained" instead. Where the criterion has no measurable outcome at all, use "Subjective Criteria". This category is for criteria that are self-contained and measurable but still allow two verdicts.
boundary: The test is whether two competent graders reading only this criterion would grade the same response differently. A criterion that is long, technical or thick with domain vocabulary is not a finding while it still has one reading: the field's terms are the task's subject, and using them precisely is what a criterion is for. So report a second reading you can state -- name both readings and a response that one accepts and the other rejects. A second reading has to be forced by the wording, not available to a determined reader, and a finding has to be able to say three things. The reading turns on something the criterion's own words or the task's material put there -- a referent with two candidates in the material, an ordering the criterion never states, a term the material uses two ways, a clause that could be an aside or part of the ask; reading an ordinary phrase in a sense it does not ordinarily carry is not a second reading. The dividing response is one a correct answer would produce, rather than one built to split the readings. And a reading is not settled because the prompt or the material would settle it: the definition names leaning on context the criterion does not state as this defect, and its test is two graders holding only the criterion. That list is examples and not the whole of it. A value the criterion carries inside itself -- a parenthetical, an apposition, a figure named in passing -- reads as part of the ask or as an annotation saying which thing is meant, and which it is divides correct answers only where the value conflicts with what the task's material and its stated conventions produce. Where it agrees, both readings reach the same verdict on a correct answer and the criterion is clean: naming a figure a correct answer states anyway identifies the subject rather than adding a second ask. Where it conflicts, give both numbers -- the one the conventions yield and the one the criterion carries -- and that is the finding. Where the problem is instead that the criterion cannot be evaluated against the response at all without the prompt, the reference text or another criterion it is Criteria Not Self Contained, and where it names no checkable outcome at all it is Subjective Criteria. This category is for a criterion that is checkable and correct and still admits more than one verdict. The remedy is a rewrite, and it must never be to drop a clause naming the source the answer has to come from. Where the second reading is about whether such a clause is part of the ask, say to make it explicit -- deleting it is what would remove the rubric's ability to catch an answer that reaches the right value from the wrong place, or from nowhere, which is the failure this project exists to measure. Offer the tightening remedy only. Keeping the clause is not sufficient, because a rewrite can narrow what the criterion catches without deleting anything: a remedy that replaces the firing condition with one example of it leaves every other wrong answer unpenalised. So test your own rewrite before you offer it -- name a wrong answer the criterion as written catches, and confirm the rewrite still catches it. A remedy may only make a criterion stricter or leave its reach unchanged.

name: Incorrect Criteria
definition:
Incorrect Definition:
Criterion checks for something that does not align with prompt requirements

Criterion contains a factual error or a misleading point

Example: "The response implements a sorting algorithm that runs in O(nlogn), such as selection sort"

Criterion is not an explicit requirement in the prompt and implementing it makes the response worse

Criterion is not at all related to the requests in the prompt



NOTE: Before classifying any issue as “Incorrect criteria”, see if a different, more specific error category would apply. For example, if a criterion is overly specific, you could argue that it’s “incorrect”, but it should still be counted as “Overfitting and Underfitting”.
boundary: The factual-error half of this definition is judged against the task's material and against the check that settles the fact, and not against authoring/ground_truth.md taken as given. The ground truth is the author's answer and one of the files you check: a criterion that states what the ground truth states is a factual error where the ground truth is itself inaccurate, and the finding names the statement the criterion repeats and the check that shows it is wrong. Two kinds of check settle a factual error without a judgement of the field. The first is the task contradicting itself: the criterion conflicts with the task's own material -- a figure or statement elsewhere in the ground truth, the workspace data, or another criterion in the same rubric. "Longer" where the two figures the rubric pins make it shorter, a stated difference that is not the subtraction of the two values it names, a count the workspace does not hold, an identifier or formula the criterion says a file carries when no file in the workspace carries it. Checking the workspace is looking rather than expertise, so search it before clearing a criterion that attributes a value to it, and say where you looked. Give both sides and say where each appears. The second is a recomputation: a claim wrong by arithmetic, by units, by a textbook definition, or by a condition a document in the task states -- the definition's own example, selection sort as O(n log n), is of this kind, and so is a value sized from one of a standard's conditions where the task requires every one of them. The finding shows the check -- the calculation, the conversion, the definition or the condition -- so a reader without the field's expertise can confirm it. A claim the field contradicts is filed on the same terms, where a check you can show settles it. The definition's limbs on a criterion that does not align with the prompt's requirements are judged against the prompt as written and are untouched by this. Where settling a doubt takes a judgement that neither the task's material nor a check you can show settles -- whether a difference is meaningful in the field, whether a method is the accepted one -- do not file it: write it in `notes` as a doubt, naming the criterion, its claim and your doubt. It is printed in the report unscored. Where the criterion is correct but its wording admits a second verdict, that is Dense or Ambiguous Phrasing, and where it rests on a qualifier with no stated standard it is Subjective Criteria; neither is this category. So a finding has to name the fact the criterion gets wrong and the material or the check that settles it, and say where the ground truth stands on it. Check the graded result before claiming the criterion cost a correct response something: where the response earned the criterion, the harm is hypothetical and has to be stated as hypothetical rather than as what happened. The ground truth can disagree with itself, and where it does, "what the ground truth states" is not one thing. Reconcile any figure it gives more than once: a value in a table and the same value restated in prose, a quantity derived in one section and referred back to in another. Where the two disagree, the criterion is judged against the side the task's own data supports -- the table, the derivation, the file the figure came out of -- and not against whichever side the author happened to restate. A criterion copying the unsupported side carries a factual error and is a finding here, and the finding gives both figures, says where each appears, and says which the data settles. Say in the same finding that the ground truth is inconsistent, because the criterion is the symptom and the material is where it has to be fixed. Where the criterion copies the supported side, the inconsistency still belongs in the report and the criterion is clean.

name: Overfitting and Underfitting
definition:
Overfitting Definition:
Criteria that are overly specific, inflexible or too rigid - they incorrectly reject a subset of valid implementations

Underfitting Definition:
Criteria that are overly broad, permissive or loose - they accept valid implementations, but also incorrectly accept invalid implementations too


Criteria must be flexible enough to accept different valid implementations. Note that criteria can mention specific answers as long as they are provided as examples in any way. i.e. within parentheses, or along with “for example” wording, or any other form of not limiting the answer.

Conversely, criteria must not be too permissive or overly broad, such that they would also accept invalid implementations along with valid implementations.
boundary: The definition's test for overfitting is that the criterion incorrectly rejects a subset of valid implementations, so a finding has to name a valid implementation it rejects. Absence from the prompt is not that test: a criterion a correct response satisfies rejects nothing, however unrequested it is. The unrequested criterion that costs a correct response something is in Incorrect Criteria's own definition, so send it there rather than widening this one. Where the task's own data determines a single answer there is no subset of valid implementations left to reject, so naming that answer outright is not overfitting even where the prompt never restates it; the allowance for specific answers given as examples is for asks that more than one answer satisfies. Read authoring/ground_truth.md before filing: what it gives as the answer is determined, including where it is reachable only through a paper the prompt sends the model out to, and a criterion demanding all of a set the ground truth lists is asking for completeness rather than rejecting a valid answer -- a response supplying part of that set is incomplete, not a valid implementation being turned away. That holds only while the ground truth does: where the answer it gives rests on an inaccurate statement, the criterion copying it is an Incorrect Criteria finding naming that statement, not a determined answer. Where the workspace alone supports less than the ground truth asserts, that is a gap in the material and belongs in the report as one, not as a finding against the criterion. Report overly specific when several answers are equally valid and the criterion picks one without saying why. Underfitting needs its case named the same way: give the invalid implementation the criterion accepts. A criterion that requires the response to state something without constraining what it states is that case rather than a pass. Requiring the response to have read or analysed the workspace evidence is never overfitting, and a criterion that cannot be satisfied without opening a file or reading an image rejects no valid implementation -- engaging the evidence is what the task is for, so the remedy for a vague evidence criterion is to say what it must state, never to make it reachable without the evidence. A criterion pinning a figure to the decimal is the overfitting case wherever its siblings do not, and this is a comparison across the rubric rather than a judgement about any one criterion. Where one criterion demands a value to four decimal places with no tolerance and another in the same rubric asks for the same kind of quantity "or equivalent to within rounding", the stricter one rejects an answer the rubric elsewhere accepts -- and a correct response rounding at a different step is exactly that valid implementation. So read the rubric's other numeric criteria before clearing one, name the sibling that grants the allowance, and give the rounding a correct answer could produce that the pinned criterion turns down. Its bound: where every numeric criterion in the rubric pins its figure the same way, there is no inconsistency and the precision is the task's own convention, which is not this category's business.

name: Overlapping/Redundant Criteria
definition:
Overlapping/Redundant Definition:
Criterion that is either completely redundant because other criteria completely encompass the former or multiple criteria that check for the same thing partly

This can also apply to criteria which have direct semantic overlap with oppositely weighted criteria. AS LONG AS: The negative criteria is not a proven agent hallucination. 08/21

E.g., “The agent only references information obtained from tool calls” (positive) and “The agent references information external to tool call outputs” (negative)

These criteria are essentially evaluating the same aspect—just with different weight polarities.

Count each completely redundant criteria as one moderate issue or count multiple overlapping criteria as one moderate issue


Redundant Scenario:
Criteria 1: Response does a, b, c
Criteria 2: Response does a, b

Overlap Scenario:
Criteria 1: Response does a, b, c
Criteria 2: Response does b, c, d

Note that this applies to cases where two criteria independently assess the same elements, not when a single criterion introduces and specifies related requirements. ("The response follows best code practices by ensuring that each line is under 79 characters" is acceptable.)
boundary: A finding has to name the element that both criteria assess. Count as the definition's two scenarios do. A criterion is completely redundant when every response that satisfies another criterion also satisfies it, because all of its elements are among the other's -- "Response does a, b" beside "Response does a, b, c". That holds however natural the pair looks: a check that the response names something sits under a check that it names it with the correct value, and a check of one item sits under a check that names that item among a list of required ones, so the smaller criterion is redundant. Each completely redundant criterion is one Moderate issue, filed against it, so four checks contained in one criterion are four issues. Criteria that overlap without either containing the other -- "Response does a, b, c" beside "Response does b, c, d" -- are one Moderate issue for the whole group, filed against one of them and naming the rest. Before filing either, test containment in both directions with a response that earns one criterion and not the other: where one exists each way, neither contains the other. The opposite-polarity case is the definition's own example: a negative that is the positive stated the other way round, penalising the failure of exactly what the positive rewards in the same terms, so that the two are essentially evaluating the same aspect with different weight polarities. A negative naming a particular wrong claim -- a named distractor, a wrong figure, a specific way of getting the answer wrong -- is not that, even though a response making the claim also fails the positive: it assesses whether the response fell for that claim, which no positive does. The proviso excludes the pair only where the negative is a proven agent hallucination, and proven means the agent committed it: the negative fired against this run's answer. Read the grades in run_removals/evaluation_results.json and the model's answer to tell, and where the recorded verdict and the answer disagree, the answer decides -- say so in the finding. An opposite-polarity pair whose negative did not fire is this overlap, and it counts as one Moderate issue, filed against the negative. A criterion that draws a conclusion from two others is not encompassed by them. Stating two facts and stating what follows from them together are different behaviours, and a response can earn both premises and never join them, so the conjunction is assessed by nothing else. The reverse does not hold: where the conclusion's own text requires the response to state a premise, the criterion stating that premise is contained in it and is redundant. One pair is outside this category in both directions: a criterion checking a value or verdict in the response, and one checking that the same value or verdict is carried into an output file the prompt asks for. The weights guidance calls these an accuracy check and a carryover check, treats the pair as ordinary rubric structure, and prices only the carryover's weight, which the weights group judges. File neither half here, and that holds where the grader read both from the file: which place it read is a question about the grade, not about the rubric.

name: Incorrect Weights - Major
definition:
(this is a major weighting error, but in the overall count it counts as a moderate issue)

Incorrect Weights - Major Definition:
Criteria that are objectively incorrectly weighted by two levels, e.g., 1 is selected when 5 is appropriate or vice versa

Criteria are categorized into one of 6 weight buckets: 5/3/1/-1/-3/-5, see the table below for descriptions and examples of each weight category.
boundary: A weight you would call borderline is not a finding. The buckets price a criterion into a band, so a weight one step from where you would have put it is inside the band the author was working in, and saying so and filing anyway reports an author's judgement as a defect. File where the weight is outside the bucket the criterion's own content puts it in, and quote the bucket that puts it there. Judge each criterion against the buckets on its own content, and never against a budget for the set of criteria covering one ask. There is no such budget. A prompt ask answered by several criteria is priced by pricing each of them, so a criterion that meets the +5 description is +5 however many of its neighbours also do, and a total you find high is not evidence against any member of it. Arguing from the group's total is how this category produced its false findings: every one of them conceded the criterion was right read against the buckets alone. Erring toward reporting governs how much evidence a finding needs, not whether a weight is in its bucket, and it never turns a weight you have cleared into a finding. One case is a finding on the arithmetic rather than the buckets: a negative criterion whose penalty is outweighed by the positives it guards, so that a response which commits the error it penalises still nets positive on that ask. Coverage is told to send this here rather than file it as a missing criterion, so it is yours, and it is the guard-that-does-not-bite case that matters most on this project -- a hallucination penalty a response can absorb and still profit from is a penalty in name only. Show the arithmetic: the positives on the ask, the penalty against them, and the net a wrong answer keeps.

name: Incorrect Weights - Minor
definition:
Incorrect Weights - Minor Definition:
Criteria that are objectively incorrectly weighted by one level. e.g, 1v3 or 3v5 scenarios


Criteria are categorized into one of 6 weight buckets: 5/3/1/-1/-3/-5, see the table below for descriptions and examples of each weight category.

06/08 NOTE: When an “accuracy check” is already covered by a Weight-5 criterion—e.g., “The final response reports that the total payment sum is $123.45”—, a “carryover check” (which checks that the value is correctly represented in an artifact) can be slightly “underweighted” without penalty. (This does not apply to egregious Weight discrepancies, i.e., Weight: 5 -> 1.)

Example:
Prompt: “How much did I pay for ____? Send this total to John in an email.”

C1: “The final response reports that the total payment sum is $123.45” {Weight: 5}

C2: “The email sent to John states that the total payment sum is $123.45” {Weight: 3}

Ideally, the Weight for C2 should be 5.

However, as the value has already been checked by C1—a Weight-5 criterion—, this “underweighting” does not need to be penalized.

(On the other hand, if C2’s Weight was assigned as 1, then this could be penalized with “Incorrect Weights - Major”.)
